  "square emphasizes modern facilities and fewer temporary classrooms more than circle": "Square notes tangible infrastructure: \"KHS facilities are new and nice, I don't see trailers as much as the other district,\" whereas Circle provides no comparable details about campus facilities or recent construction.",
  "square describes explicit STEM and engineering programming (including robotics) more than circle": "Square states \"they will offer engineering classes as well... We have a great STEM program and robotics team!\" while Circle focuses on athletics and performing arts with no comparable descriptions of school STEM curricula or robotics programs.",
  "circle highlights distinctive performing arts achievements more than square": "Circle cites concrete performing arts accolades: \"Vox chorus won at 2012 World Choir Games and Jazz & Concert band flourish..   "square presents clearly defined graduation/course requirements that circle does not": "Square specifies graduation requirements: \"Students must take 2 years of a foreign language to graduate along w/ 40 hrs of community service,\" whereas Circle discusses holistic formation and \"Grad at Grad\" virtues but does not list specific graduation/course mandates.",
  "circle indicates a school culture with high extracurricular/time demands more than square": "Circle warns about time commitment and involvement expectations: \"If you want to leave at 3:00, don't come to Prep.   "square portrays teacher quality as consistently rigorous while circle reports mixed teacher quality": "Square states \"The teachers are tough and good\" and describes rigorous sequences built into the curriculum, whereas Circle explicitly notes variability: \"the teachers in the school are either amazing, or just really bad\" and reviewers describe both great and not-so-great teachers."

["{
  "circle reports more persistent bullying and social exclusion (including non-local students) than square": "Circle states explicitly that \"there is still bullying going on if you do not fit in\" and recounts a personal case: \"I was bullied like crazy because I'm not from granite falls... it got so bad I had to switch school,\" whereas Square only mentions general school problems and says \"Problems seem to be dealt with accordingly,\" with no sustained account of exclusion-driven bullying or student transfers.",
  "circle describes vocational and dual-enrollment career pathways more than square": "Circle names specific career/college-readiness programs—\"Running Start and Sno-Isle technical programs\"—and praises them: \"Students can actually get what they need to get a jump on their careers!\" Square contains no mention of vocational, technical, or dual-enrollment programs.",
  "circle highlights a strong band program more than square": "Circle explicitly praises extracurriculars with \"they had a great band program,\" while Square only references general athletic parent involvement and does not single out music or band quality.",
  "square shows higher explicit parental involvement in academics and athletics than circle": "Square states \"There is high parent involvement on both an academic and atheletic level,\" whereas Circle refers to a caring small district and community openness but does not assert high parental involvement in academics or athletics specifically.",
  "square emphasizes staff focus on teaching respect and helping students excel more than circle": "Square asserts that \"The staff does a good job at teaching respect and helping students excel in areas of interest\" and that there are \"more caring teachers than not,\" whereas Circle’s comments focus on student social dynamics and programs rather than teacher pedagogy or classroom support.",
  "square reports that school addresses problems both proactively and reactively more than circle": "Square explicitly claims the school \"addresses problems both proactively and reactively\" and that \"Problems seem to be dealt with accordingly,\" while Circle documents ongoing issues (bullying) and does not describe effective problem-resolution processes.",
  "square contains a reported historical lack of teacher leadership not present in circle": "Square includes the line \"When my child attended Warren County high school years ago, I observed a lack of leadership among the teachers,\" a specific claim about past staff leadership gaps that Circle does not make."
}"]

["{
  "circle exhibits pervasive grade inflation and mandatory minimum grades whereas square does not": "Multiple reviewers in circle state grading is artificially high: “NO child can fail, NO child receives less than a C,” “Ms.Joyner doesn't allow the teachers to give any grade below a C,” and one reviewer reports deliberately failing tests yet “still ended up with straight A's.” Square contains no comparable claim about schoolwide enforced minimum grades.",
  "circle lacks scheduled physical education and recess while square describes athletics and campus facilities": "Circle repeatedly reports the absence of PE/recess: “there is no curriculum for gym,” “no recess or gym,” and “My child has spent years without recess.” Square emphasizes a strong campus and athletics/opportunities: “amazing campus,” “Truly a great school! From student life to academics to athletics!”",
  "circle reports many teachers are unqualified or former students while square reports mostly caring or certified teachers with some variability": "Circle reviewers allege uncertified staff and former-student hires: “most of the teachers aren't qualified,” “Some of them are former students,” and “they can not teach anywhere else.” Square reviewers say “some teachers are caring” and “All the teachers I had were wonderful,” though they note uneven lesson planning.",
  "circle reports outdated instructional materials and lack of classroom technology whereas square does not raise this issue": "Circle reviewers cite technology and materials gaps: “the lack of technology in the classrooms,” “A write and wipe board as the only means of teaching,” and “a text book that was very old and out of date.” Square contains no mention of obsolete textbooks or systemic lack of classroom technology.",
  "circle reports poor academic rigor and college unpreparedness while square reports stronger college pathways and honors/AP opportunities": "Circle reviewers warn graduates were unprepared: “plenty of Alumni's who came back for tutoring because they could barely READ!” and “after graduating and going on to college, they struggled severely because of what and how they were taught at MCSCS.” Square reviewers describe college progression and advanced classes: “If you want to get involved there are more than enough opportunities,” “I, and many of my classmates, went straight to a university,” and references to honors/high achieving classes.",
  "square reports on-campus violence, bullying, and mishandled harassment incidents more than circle": "Square reviewers repeatedly highlight serious bullying and violence: “huge spark in violence within the campus,” “bullying it is a BIG problem,” and complaints that harassment was not handled correctly. Circle mentions misbehavior interfering with classes but lacks repeated, campus-level violence claims.",
  "circle emphasizes classroom-level disruptive behavior affecting concentration more than square": "Several circle reviewers note students misbehaving in class and teachers constantly stopping to correct them: “My child complains that she can not concentrate in class because the students are misbehaving and the teacher has to constantly stop to correct them.” Square focuses more on larger-scale bullying and campus divisions than this specific classroom concentration issue.",
  "square reports poor communication and event organization for families whereas circle highlights lack of assessment feedback to parents": "Square complaints focus on event communication: “NO ONE tells us what events are going on,” and “They are very unorganized when it comes to pictures.” Circle reviewers specifically note absence of assessment feedback: “I have never received a graded test paper or any other measure of proof that my child is learning anything,” indicating different communication failures.",
  "square reports large class sizes explicitly while circle does not mention class size": "Square provides concrete class ratio details: “Classes are approx. 38 -1 if not 41-1,” whereas circle contains no similar numeric class size statements.",
  "circle reports administrative policies enforcing lenient grading and frequent staff/administration turnover more than square": "Circle reviewers cite administrative enforcement and churn: “Ms. Joyner and her band of cronies are hustling the state,” “the teaching staff and administration changes every year,” and teachers allegedly “tried to encourage me to attend another school.” Square mentions isolated staff problems (e.g., a rude librarian or mishandled incidents) but not systemic administrative policy enforcing grades or high turnover.",
  "square highlights a more visibly diverse student culture with achievement stratification while circle emphasizes uniform grade outcomes masking real ability differences": "Square reviewers describe a divided student body and feeder-school differences: “there is a MAJOR division in the student body,” and “the two feeder schools are also very different.” Circle repeatedly argues everyone receives high grades regardless of effort, masking skill gaps: “I was always an all A B student but when I started going there all of a sudden im getting straight A's in subjects that I know darn well I never did work,” and “she brags about 99% of kids that goes to her school goes to college BUT do they get through? NO!”"
}"]

["{
  "circle provides a formal Talent Development special-education program for students with mild learning disabilities more than square": "Circle explicitly describes a dedicated program: \"Talent Development... created for children with MILD learning disabilities\" and praises individualized outcomes from it, whereas Square states struggling students are given only superficial help and that \"if the child has learning issues... the child doesn't stand a chance,\" indicating no comparable specialized program.",
  "circle delivers individualized instruction and low student/teacher ratios with one-on-one assistants more than square": "Circle praises \"a highly individualized approach... low student/teacher ratio with an assistant available for one-on-one help,\" while Square reports that \"If you struggle at all you are given material to help you pass the course, but not learn the course,\" showing lack of individualized remediation.",
  "circle demonstrates faith-based pastoral care and daily teacher mentoring (including prayer) more than square": "Circle states \"His teachers have prayed with him daily\" and \"You can go to any teacher in the school and they will help you and pray with you,\" whereas Square contains no description of faith-based mentoring and instead highlights staff hostility.",
  "circle reports observable positive postsecondary academic outcomes for students more than square": "Circle notes concrete postsecondary success: \"My child graduated from this program... continued to college, earning a spot on the deans list,\" while Square provides no alumni or college-success evidence and focuses on current classroom problems.",
  "square reports adult-led bullying, staff ridicule, and racial discrimination more than circle": "Square alleges severe staff misconduct: students \"are laughed at, made fun of behind their backs by staff\" and \"if a different race the child doesn't stand a chance,\" and names the \"school resource officer is a bully,\" whereas Circle predominantly describes supportive teacher behavior with only isolated complaints.",
  "square emphasizes Common Core alignment and advancement-by-performance with minimal mastery support more than circle": "Square says \"Common Core material is widespread\" and \"if you do well you advance. If you struggle... you are given material to help you pass the course, but not learn the course,\" indicating performance-driven advancement and superficial remediation not described in Circle.",
  "circle reports more proactive communication and responsiveness between administration/teachers and parents than square": "Circle asserts \"The administration communicates very well with the parents\" and multiple statements that \"Teachers will work with you to help foster your education,\" whereas Square contains no claims of responsive parent communication and instead cites staff antagonism.",
  "circle promotes inclusive athletics regardless of ability more than square": "Circle explicitly states \"The sports programs are encouraged regardless of ability,\" while Square contains no mention of inclusive athletic opportunities and focuses on negative staff behavior and academics.",
  "circle enforces strict tuition/withdrawal and records-withholding policies more than square": "Circle includes a complaint that the school \"would only refund a fraction of his tuition\" and that they \"would have withheld his records\" until payment, documenting a restrictive financial/records policy that Square does not mention.",
  "square references external ranking and comparative proficiency metrics more than circle": "Square cites objective metrics: \"ranked by US News and World Report at #70 in the state... bronze award winner\" and \"Higher than Tipton, Alexandria and Frankton in mathematics proficiency,\" whereas Circle contains no external ranking or comparative proficiency statistics."
}"]

["{
  "square reports administrative mismanagement and poor responsiveness whereas circle does not": "Square contains multiple accounts of school leaders failing to communicate and take responsibility: \"no one returns calls\" and \"reaching out to the main superintendent and that got me no where,\" plus accusations that the school board \"pretty much cover each other's behinds.\" Circle offers no report of administrative failures.",
  "square documents severe student safety problems (bullying, gang violence, drugs, fights) whereas circle does not": "Square explicitly warns \"A very dangerous school they have gang violence at this school and a lot of bullying and a lot of fights and too much drug problems,\" while circle only notes that \"the people at Holland aren't very friendly,\" with no mention of violence, drugs, or bullying.",
  "square describes concrete academic placement and credit errors that harmed graduation outcomes whereas circle does not": "Square alleges the school \"dropped her down to needing 22 credits and for 1/2 a credit short they benched her\" and admits staff changed her math placement (\"took her out of Geometry and put her in Math Models\") causing inappropriate summer school and preventing graduation; circle contains no such outcome-level errors.",
  "square reports extreme negative student mental-health consequences tied to school actions whereas circle does not": "Square links school failures to serious harm: the reviewer says their daughter \"was so close to ending her life\" and that the situation \"made her spiral again,\" indicating acute mental-health consequences tied to school handling; circle has no mental-health claims.",
  "square describes widespread lack of staff care but also names specific teachers who go above and beyond whereas circle gives only a general unfriendly assessment": "Square states \"There are very few staff that actually care about the students\" but also praises individuals by name (\"My english teacher Mrs. Ellis... She's gone above and beyond\" and \"Mrs.Parker... Mrs. Blankman\"), while circle provides only a blanket comment that \"the people at Holland aren't very friendly.\"",
  "square attributes low extracurricular participation and poor school spirit to restrictive policies and district culture more than circle": "Square links weak participation and spirit to rules and culture: \"Her rules are over-the-top strict and unreasonable. $1 fine to wear a hat for a school spirit day?... less then 25% of the entire school participates\" and cites \"a minimal amount of clubs & extracurricular activities,\" whereas circle only notes \"Many Holland sports have low participation\" without describing policy causes.",
  "square reports pervasive student behavioral and classroom disruption problems to a greater extent than circle": "Square complains students \"aren't focused on the future,\" classes are \"full of obnoxious students who don't shut up,\" and claims \"a good 90% of students possess no discipline,\" while circle does not describe widespread behavioral disruption beyond calling people \"not very friendly.\"",
  "circle offers an explicit inter-school comparison praising another district whereas square does not": "Circle opens with a comparative endorsement: \"East Aurora is a much better school,\" directly comparing schools; square focuses entirely on problems at the reviewed school without naming a better alternative.",
  "circle focuses criticism narrowly on sports participation and social unfriendliness whereas square reports a wide range of concrete institutional and safety problems": "Circle's complaints are limited to \"Many Holland sports have low participation\" and that \"the people at Holland aren't very friendly,\" while square enumerates multiple institutional issues (administration, credits, discipline, bullying, gangs, drugs, restrictive rules, lack of clubs) indicating systemic problems beyond social unfriendliness or sports."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports more unchecked student misbehavior and bullying than square": "Circle explicitly states 'Bulliying runs rampant and unchecked by the staff' and documents chronic classroom disruption ('2 cell phones rang, students goofing off and talking... the teacher never missed a beat'), whereas Square only mentions 'a few trouble makers that need to be dealt with'—a milder, isolated discipline concern.",
  "circle reports greater administrative indifference and refusal to address complaints than square": "Circle documents leadership failing to act ('The principal and assistant principal are disgraces... They simply refuse to acknowledge any problems') and an assistant principal dismissing a recording ('That is the discretion of the teacher...'), while Square highlights 'Awesome Teachers and a wonderful community feel' and gratitude toward staff with no comparable claims of administrative dismissal.",
  "circle describes concrete assessment and exam quality problems that square does not": "Circle complains 'Final exams are a joke' and that 'Study guides were no more than cheat sheets with fill in the blanks and used during exams,' indicating compromised assessment integrity; Square instead notes effective honors classes and college placement ('I got into my college of choice because of their dedication'), showing no parallel critique of assessment practices.",
  "square reports stronger community support and positive student outcomes more than circle": "Square emphasizes community solidarity and outcomes—'People rally around each other in time of need,' 'I got into my college of choice' and 'Awesome Teachers'—whereas Circle contains many reports of community fracture, parental frustration, and mixed student outcomes.",
  "circle reports higher teacher turnover and staffing instability than square": "Circle says 'They have teachers coming and going left and right, TOO many rules' and 'we have lost a lot of teachers,' while Square offers praise for teachers ('Great teachers... extremely caring and helpful') and contains no claims of widespread staff turnover.",
  "circle reports stricter policies and more restrictive student privileges than square": "Circle repeatedly notes heavy rules and lost privileges ('TOO many rules... we as students have no privileges... They cant even have water in class'), and even military-like operation ('This school is ran like a military school'), whereas Square criticizes only a softer issue—calling for 'tougher... discipline'—not blanket restrictive policies.",
  "circle highlights strong JROTC and drill team programs more than square": "Multiple Circle reviewers praise JROTC and drill team ('the JROTC is probably one of the best programs... the drill team and basketball team are outstanding'), while Square praises arts and honors programs and does not mention JROTC or drill.",
  "circle reports systemic failures in handling attendance notes, 504/IEP accommodations, and formal supports more than square": "Circle reports specific procedural failures—'the attendance lady will not accept notes half the time signed by a doctor' and 'Their 504/IEP sucks!'—whereas Square contains only a single homebound-tutor complaint ('home tutor teachers refuse to give tutor work and no communication') but no broader claims about 504/IEP or attendance systems.",
  "circle documents a perceived decline in school quality over time that square does not": "Circle states 'This school has gone from good to poor since the beginning of the second year of opening' and 'it has gotten worse with each passing year,' while Square offers present-tense positive reflections with no narrative of multi-year decline.",
  "circle reports inconsistent grading scales and ambiguous grading policy practices more than square": "Circle specifically complains 'And the grading scale is different' and accuses the school of 'make up extra memorandums to get away from the POLICY they hand out to each student,' whereas Square makes no note of grading-scale inconsistency.",
  "circle emphasizes social exclusivity and clique dynamics more than square": "Circle warns 'It has become a very exclusive school and if you aren't in the clique you're not welcome there,' describing social exclusion impacting students and parents, while Square only notes general 'favoritisms granted to those who \"know someone\"' framed as common and minor."
}"]

["{
  "circle enforces stricter phone and conduct rules than square": "Circle states an explicit phone ban and stricter rules: \"there are no phones allowed at any time, especially not at mass, and the teachers make sure of it\" and \"the rules at Rock are more strict than most other schools,\" whereas Square contains no mention of a schoolwide phone or similar conduct ban.",
  "circle reports virtually no physical fights and faster resolution of theft than square": "Circle repeatedly asserts low incidence and fast handling of misconduct: \"I have seen ZERO fights... theft? if there is any theft Dean Alvey or a faculty member clear it up quickly,\" while Square makes no similar claims of near-zero fights or dean-led rapid resolution.",
  "circle emphasizes college preparation and scholarship readiness more than square": "Circle claims explicit college- and scholarship-oriented outcomes: \"this school will prepare your son to achieve a scholarship\" and \"He is well prepared for college... Excellent preparation for success at college and in life,\" whereas Square focuses more on course load and programs rather than claiming direct scholarship preparation.",
  "square subjects students to heavy AP and frequent standardized testing for freshmen more than circle": "Square describes academic overload and repeated testing: \"They give their students tons of AP classes... testing for freshmen... ranging from 10-15 big tests that they had to pass,\" a curricular/testing pressure not described in Circle.",
  "square reports front office and lost and found responsiveness problems while circle reports responsive faculty discipline": "Square calls out administrative operational lapses: \"Wish the front office would put some afford to return the lost and fond items to the kids,\" whereas Circle highlights prompt faculty/dean intervention in incidents: \"Dean Alvey or a faculty member clear it up quickly.\"",
  "circle foregrounds explicit religious formation and mass-related practices more than square": "Circle uses religious language and school ritual context: \"Ad Majorem Dei Gloriam,\" and enforces phone bans \"especially not at mass,\" and describes becoming \"religious, open to growth,\" while Square contains no reference to religion or mass.",
  "circle credits coaching for rapid individual athletic improvement while square emphasizes program legacy and rebuilding": "Circle ties athletics to individual development: \"my athletic ability has skyrocketed thanks to all Coaches,\" whereas Square highlights sport traditions and program cycles: \"WRESTLING...one of the best programs...in a rebuilding state... the football programs is very good...theyve hit the ground running.\"",
  "square reports social cliquishness among students more than circle": "Square admits social exclusivity: \"This school can be a little clique -y,\" and frames it as a normal high-school dynamic, whereas Circle emphasizes a trusting, trouble-free student community: \"we can be trusted and we don't start trouble.\"",
  "circle describes trust-based student privileges (staying late) that square does not": "Circle explains privilege tied to behavior: \"The reason we can be around school until late is because we can be trusted,\" a specific operational practice absent from Square.",
  "square highlights vocational/technical program availability and broad extracurricular offerings more than circle": "Square explicitly names \"Excel Tecc programs and clubs\" and \"lots of extracurricular activities,\" indicating vocational and broad activity options, while Circle focuses on athletics, academics, and religious formation without mentioning vocational programs or a broad club ecosystem."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports a small, close-knit school community with teachers who know students more than square": "Circle states plainly, \"The teachers know all the students and have a real connection with them\" and \"Halstead is a smaller school,\" whereas square repeatedly describes an over-populated environment (\"thousands of kids,\" \"over-populated suburban High Schools\") and lacks any claim of schoolwide personal familiarity.",
  "square reports frequent bullying, harassment, and hateful slurs more than circle": "Square documents pervasive bullying and hateful language — \"I've already been referred to as a r3t4rd and a f4gg0t on multiple occasions,\" \"Arbor View turns a blind eye on bullying\" — while circle contains no reports of student-on-student harassment.",
  "square reports administrative mishandling of discipline and scorn for reporting problems more than circle": "Square gives multiple examples of poor administrative responses to complaints, e.g. a dean saying, \"Nobody likes a snitch,\" and a student who apologized but was still \"blocked from attending class,\" whereas circle offers no claims of disciplinary failures or retaliation.",
  "square reports abusive or unprofessional teacher behavior (cursing, expulsion, labeling) more than circle": "Square recounts teachers \"cursing at students,\" a teacher who was \"blatantly disrespectful\" and repeated removal from class, and teachers who \"label students,\" while circle emphasizes teachers' positive connections and has no mention of abusive conduct.",
  "square reports inconsistent teacher quality and wide variability in instruction more than circle": "Square repeatedly notes \"some really good teachers, we've had some horrible teachers\" and \"They are either really nice or very abusive,\" indicating high variability in teaching quality; circle uniformly praises teachers and reports no such inconsistency.",
  "square reports systemic student tracking and misplacement that impede student improvement more than circle": "Square asserts the school 'tracks' students causing placement mismatches (\"being put in classes that don't match her new resolve to succeed\"), whereas circle does not mention tracking or forced placement issues.",
  "square reports significant maintenance and pest problems despite facility praise more than circle": "Square contains explicit reports of infestations: \"I've heard reports from several of cockroaches... cafeteria and other classrooms were infested,\" even as another reviewer calls the \"facility is amazing though!\" Circle mentions nothing about facilities or pests.",
  "square reports digital access and homework policy problems that create inequity more than circle": "Square criticizes technology policies and homework practices that disadvantage students: \"If the school blocks the web site... students to have to pull out their I phone or androids... Not all students can afford data plans,\" and says computer-based work \"feels like a way to reduce the amount of work the teacher does grading;\" circle does not reference digital-access or homework inequity.",
  "square reports higher incidence of substance use and behavior-control problems more than circle": "Square explicitly flags \"high drug use\" and poor behavior control—\"They are not effective in behavior control\"—while circle contains no mention of substance use or chronic behavior-management issues.",
  "square reports athletic favoritism and problematic coaching culture more than circle": "Square describes athletic culture problems and favoritism: \"If your child is a star athlete they will have no problem... The head coach for varsity is arrogant! He will not even talk to you unless your kid is one of his star players,\" whereas circle makes no mention of athletics.",
  "square reports curricular gaps in practical life-skills classes more than circle": "Square criticizes a course called Independent Living for failing to teach finance and budgeting (\"All they actually do is teach the student how to sew and cook... didn't even learn how to write a check or create a budget\"), while circle praises offerings generally and gives no complaints about curricular content.",
  "square reports alleged staff financial misconduct affecting students more than circle": "Square alleges serious misconduct: \"The teaches abscond funds from the student atheletes on the pretence of traveling for sport events,\" a type of operational/ethical problem absent from circle.",
  "square documents formal accommodations for disabilities and transgender students whereas circle does not mention them": "Square notes concrete supports: \"There are steps I can take with the administration to help me keep up... accommodations for trans youth... options to change the name/gender listed on your Infinite Campus,\" while circle makes no mention of specific special-education or LGBTQ accommodations."
}"]

["{
  "circle exhibits stronger, centralized principal leadership and student/parent advocacy than square": "Circle is dominated by repeated accounts of one principal (Alan/Mr. Potts) who ‘changed the school,’ ‘attends all sporting events,’ ran ‘Coffee with Potts,’ and inspired mass parent/student protest (‘#savepotts’, ‘students are protested’, ‘If they do not renew his contract I am pulling my kids out’), whereas Square contains no analogous, sustained narrative of a single leader or organized community defense.",
  "circle reports an administrative discipline and safety turnaround more than square": "Multiple Circle reviews say the ‘new administration cracked down on discipline, as well as attendance,’ ‘got rid of most if not all drug gangs, lowered the number of fights,’ and call the school transformed from violent to ‘SAFE and FRIENDLY,’ while Square contains statements of ongoing problems (‘Drugs, cursing, horrible teachers, ... fights every single day!’) and no clear description of a successful schoolwide crackdown.",
  "circle attributes measurable academic improvements to leadership more than square": "Circle reviewers link leadership to academic gains: ‘test scores have improved,’ ‘The AP program has expanded,’ and ‘we are the only school that jumped 9% in our writing scores,’ framing growth as leadership-driven, whereas Square notes ‘Honors and AP Level’ offerings but frames academics as established program availability rather than recent leadership-driven improvement.",
  "circle displays organized student/parent activism around administrative decisions while square does not": "Circle contains many reports of coordinated action and protest to retain the principal (‘students protested’, ‘Bring Potts back!!!!’, ‘we will help him!’), showing organized community mobilization; Square has no comparable descriptions of protests or organized parent/student campaigns.",
  "square reports a specific faculty-on-civilian threatening incident that circle does not": "Square opens with a first-person account that ‘A tall white baldheaded man … treatened me … charged at me’ while walking after hours, an alleged staff threat of bodily harm; Circle includes no report of a staff member physically threatening a community member in that manner.",
  "square emphasizes recent facility renovation and upgraded technology more than circle": "Square explicitly states ‘With the renovation it’s like a new school’ and highlights ‘Technology, athletics, music, and social clubs are alive,’ while Circle focuses more on leadership, discipline, and culture change and less on a single renovation/technology upgrade narrative.",
  "circle highlights notable sports achievements tied to school pride more than square": "Circle repeatedly cites concrete athletic successes and their role in spirit (‘Soccer being regional champs two years in a row, Baseball winning regionals last year’ and many student comments about attending games with the principal), whereas Square mentions athletics and clubs broadly but does not emphasize multiple recent regional or state-level championships.",
  "circle contains explicit complaints about failure to implement special education accommodations (504 Plan) while square does not": "One Circle reviewer asks ‘504 Plan at Copper Canyon???? Do the teachers know about Plan 504??? … My son was supposed to take tests in a private room. This never happened,’ a concrete allegation about noncompliance with special education accommodations that is absent from Square.",
  "square describes a broader set of organized curricular and extracurricular program offerings as a selling point more than circle": "Square lists a balanced mix—‘rigorous program (Honors and AP Level)’, ‘after school activities and sports’, ‘Technology, athletics, music, and social clubs’—as evidence the school ‘has something for everyone,’ whereas Circle focuses programmatically on AP expansion and specific teams but centers its narrative on leadership-driven change rather than breadth of institutional offerings.",

["{
  "circle shows measurable academic improvement and formal recognition more than square": "Circle includes concrete outcome metrics and awards: reviewers note Antioch “passed federal benchmarkc assessments for NCLB,” was “rewarded as a 'Reward high school'” and “improved their test scores by 20% over 10 years” with an “act average for the school is a 21,” while Square contains no comparable, schoolwide performance data or official recognitions.",
  "circle reports explicit resource and facility shortages more than square": "Circle reviewers list tangible material shortfalls and building operational issues such as “The school can't even supply books to the students, or afford to make copies,” and temperature/entry problems — “this school is COLD” and “school starts at 7:15am, but they don't open the doors until 6:50am,” whereas Square mentions very little about facility or supply deficits.",
  "circle documents severe student-on-student physical violence (shooting, beatings) more than square": "Circle contains direct reports of extreme incidents: “One student was shot last year” and “I know at least one was beat down so badly at school an ambulance had to be called,” while Square only states that physical abuse is “not very common” and does not report shootings or ambulance-level assaults.",
  "square depicts normalized student substance use and permissive discipline for smoking more than circle": "Square describes pervasive substance behavior and disciplinary loopholes: “Students are often caught smoking in the bathrooms… The drug usage rate is at least 70%” and students “enjoy O.S.S. for smoking in the bathroom because they can just stay at home,” presenting substance use as normalized in ways Circle does not (Circle mentions drugs in a complaint but lacks the same normalization and OSS detail).",
  "circle reports higher teacher turnover and vacant classrooms more than square": "Circle explicitly states staffing instability: “they lose teachers faster than they can rehire so this leaves classrooms without teachers,” a concrete staffing outcome absent from Square's descriptions.",
  "square reports recent structural schedule and grading policy changes that confuse and penalize students more than circle": "Square describes system-level policy shifts that disrupt learning: “the whole school changed their grading system and we have an alternating schedule… The grading system is either a pass or a fail,” and students say “the schedule messes with your head,” whereas Circle contains no comparable district-level grading/schedule reform impacting daily student tracking.",
  "circle attributes major problems to lack of parent and community support more than square": "Circle explicitly blames community engagement gaps as a root cause: “The biggest problem at AHS and virtually all urban schools...lack of parent/community support…no one shows up [to parent/teacher conferences],” a community-level explanation not offered in Square.",
  "circle documents development of specialized academic and extracurricular programs more than square": "Circle cites programmatic expansions and hires tied to college credit and enrichment: “starting IBO LEAGUE program that gives you international college credit” and the hire of an “Associate Director of Bands… He is a gift to students,” while Square only generically mentions “updated programs” without specific advanced-program launches or notable staff additions.",
  "circle reports disciplinary inconsistency and favoritism by school leadership more than square": "Circle includes complaints about unequal enforcement: “Principals played favorites with disciplinary actions towards students,” pointing to inconsistent discipline policy application; Square criticizes administrative inaction on bullying but does not allege favoritism by leadership.",
  "square emphasizes peer clique risk and widespread mental bullying more than circle": "Square foregrounds social dynamics and psychological harm: reviewers warn a child can “fall victim to the wrong clique” and call mental abuse “VERY common,” framing peer-group risk and bullying as a dominant internal threat more strongly than Circle does."
}"]

  "circle cites a specific high-achieving alumni outcome that square does not": "Circle mentions a concrete example of alumni success: \"a girl i graduated with interviewed at Harvard Medical school,\" whereas Square offers no named or specific alumni outcomes.",
  "circle emphasizes development of life and teamwork skills more than square": "Circle explicitly claims \"the most important lessons you learn in high school are those about life and how to interact with others and work as a team,\" while Square focuses on academics, college preparation, and opportunities without highlighting life/teamwork skills.",
  "square frames opportunities as universally available to every student while circle does not": "Square claims \"There are so many opportunities offered to EVERY student here,\" whereas Circle discusses opportunities unevenly (some succeed and some complain), offering no claim of universal access.",
  "square asserts comparative academic superiority over nearby schools while circle does not make such comparisons": "Square declares it is \"the best school in the area as far as academics (compared to Southside, Northside, and Riverside),\" a direct comparative claim absent from Circle's text.",
  "circle contains temporal divergence between alumni and current student reports suggesting changing or uneven conditions over time": "Circle includes a 2007 graduate who would \"go to SVHS all over again\" and also a present student who states \"I honestly hate this school,\" indicating alumni and current-student experiences differ, a contrast not present in Square.",
  "square attributes poor student experience to student effort while circle attributes poor outcomes to school shortcomings": "Square states \"if u did not or do not enjoy your experience at WHS it is because you aren't/werent trying,\" shifting responsibility to students; Circle includes explicit blame on the school for inadequate instruction: \"Swan Valley simply cannot offer me that.\""
}"]

["{
  "circle emphasizes a strong music and band program more than square": "Circle states explicitly that \"They have a fantastic music program\" and \"The band program is excellent,\" whereas Square lists many extracurriculars (\"Athletics, Drama, Math Team, Journalism, Guardian Club, Jr. NHS and NHS\") but does not single out a standout band/music program.",
  "circle shows active administrative accommodation for IEPs and individualized academic placement whereas square does not": "Circle reports \"administration has been very accommodating for our daughter academic needs including placing her in the advanced classes ahead of schedule in order to meet the guidelines of her IEP,\" while Square contains no description of IEP accommodations or proactive individualized placement.",
  "square reports deteriorating facilities and outdated instructional resources more than circle": "Square complains of \"disintegrating infrastructure, outdated textbooks\" and \"No improvements to this school for years,\" complaints that are entirely absent from Circle's account.",
  "circle reports generally supportive and adequate teachers more than square": "Circle says \"Some of the teachers are outstanding\" and \"to date we have not run into any that are inadequate,\" while Square contains explicit accusations that \"Teachers are outrageously snotty\" and \"Unless you are in top of your class, teachers take very little interest in your child.\"",
  "square reports problematic leadership and administrative refusal to change more than circle": "Square calls school \"Leadership ... a joke\" and an \"administration that refuses to change or adapt to the changing times,\" whereas Circle describes the administration as \"very accommodating\" and responsive to student needs.",
  "square reports nepotism, favoritism, and unfair athletics selection more than circle": "Square accuses sports of being \"all about who you know\" and says \"Your child will NOT be given a fair chance to compete on just there skill level,\" a concern not raised in Circle, which instead focuses on program quality and typical student behavior.",
  "square reports staffing instability and low teacher pay more than circle": "Square mentions \"low teacher wages, high faculty turn-over,\" indicating staffing instability, while Circle makes no mention of teacher pay or turnover.",
  "square reports poor alumni giving and perceived community disengagement more than circle": "Square asks \"How much in donations comes back from former students ? There is a reason, they don't give back,\" signalling concerns about alumni financial support; Circle notes parent involvement but does not report weak alumni giving.",
  "circle shows parent involvement concentrated around a program (band) more than square": "Circle notes \"parents are involved, but it could be simply because of the large number of parents involved with the band program,\" indicating program-driven parental engagement, whereas Square's references to community are more general (\"SPM becomes an extension of your family\") without tying involvement to a single program.",
  "square highlights breadth and perceived decline in institutional outcomes (dropout rates, rising tuition) more than circle": "Square alleges \"record drop-out rates\" and criticizes \"tuition continues to rise\" despite \"No improvements to this school for years,\" while Circle reports \"an above average experience\" and gives no indication of worsening student outcomes or tuition-related deterioration.",
  "square reports inconsistent teacher support internally (both neglect and exceptional extra help) while circle reports consistently adequate support": "Within Square some reviewers claim \"Don't expect extra help for your child\" and \"teachers take very little interest,\" while other reviewers brag teachers \"come in at 6:15am for a help session\" and \"staying to assist with projects after school,\" showing internal inconsistency; Circle however reports a steady pattern: \"The teachers are great\" and \"to date we have not run into any that are inadequate.\"",
  "square emphasizes expansion and strength of AP and varied course offerings more than circle, while circle emphasizes accelerating individual students into advanced classes": "Square asserts \"They AP classes offered to the upper classman are some of the best in the country, with new classes being added every year,\" indicating breadth and growth of advanced offerings; Circle instead highlights administrative placement of an individual student into \"advanced classes ahead of schedule\" to meet IEP needs, emphasizing individualized acceleration rather than program breadth."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports failures in special education and 504 implementation that harm learning while square does not": "Circle contains multiple concrete allegations: “don't expect [a 504 plan] to be followed very well,” and a parent describes removing her child after mainstreaming experiments where “special education children were being experimentally assimilated in, and because of these two children, it was impossible for her to learn.” Square makes no mention of special education or 504 issues.",
  "circle portrays administration and school board as unresponsive and favoring insiders while square presents administration as improvement-oriented": "Circle alleges administrators and the board ignore parent input and play favorites: “The school board does not want to hear negative input,” and “Leadership in the district is more about who you know not about what is best.” Square explicitly says “The district's administration is dynamic and is always looking for ways to improve the student's educational experience.”",
  "circle reports bullying, student rudeness, and safety concerns while square reports students get along": "Circle includes first‑hand claims of bullying and unsafe feelings: “I don't not feel safe here… I will be switching schools,” and “Students are rude… if you don't do sports you're a nothing.” Square states the opposite interpersonal climate: “The population is diverse…and yet all students get along.”",
  "square reports greater student diversity while circle reports limited diversity due to rural setting": "Square says explicitly that “The population is diverse and represent many different cultures,” whereas circle notes the opposite demographic constraint: “Also, it should be noted this school is in the middle of a very rural town, so diversity is not promoted.”",
  "square reports strong teacher/staff commitment while circle reports teachers who don't teach and poor classroom practices": "Square: “The teachers and staff are committed to doing everything necessary to achieve success for all students.” Circle contains accusations of poor instruction and mismanagement: “teachers who don't actually teach,” and a teacher who “gave a series of tests…then called it a project…made it worth 40% of the grade,” lowering many students' grades.",
  "circle reports PTA and parental input being ignored while square implies cooperative parent/staff relationships": "Circle recounts parent advocacy being dismissed: “The PTA and myself have an interest…but what is the point of a PTA if the school does not listen?” Square emphasizes alignment between staff and community goals without reporting ignored parent input.",
  "circle documents student outmigration to other districts for curricular choice and support while square does not mention this": "Circle states concretely: “Many kids, including mine, are going to other area schools because of limited class choices,” and several reviewers mention their children switched and ‘have never turned back.’ Square contains no reports of families leaving the district.",
  "circle reports contested pedagogical shifts and technology adoption that worry parents while square mentions no such shifts": "Circle criticizes district moves to new methods and tech: “The districts moving to a Projected Based learning style…Technology have literally taken over the whole school this year and education has gone way down.” Square makes no reference to pedagogical changes or technology concerns.",
  "circle reports documented low academic performance and poor district rankings while square claims academics are top notch": "Circle cites an external measure: “Schoolcraft was 443 out of 540 michigan districts,” and multiple reviewers say students aren’t learning; square asserts the opposite: “Academics are top notch.”",
  "square highlights extracurricular and athletic breadth positively while circle reports athletics as a dominant social gatekeeper and mixed priority": "Square praises extracurriculars: “there are many athletic programs or other extracurricular programs for the student to engage in.” Circle contains mixed commentary—some praise sports (“Out sports program is amazing”) but also describes sports culture excluding non‑athletes: “Students are rude, if you don't do sports you're a nothing,” and warns athletics may overshadow academics: “you might win on the football field but you're losing in the classroom.”",
  "circle reports fiscal and facilities controversies tied to building projects and taxes while square only notes aging facilities": "Both mention facilities, but circle adds conflict over spending: “Taxes are too high…The school wants to do additional building projects even though the enrollment hasn't increased,” whereas square only notes a physical shortcoming: “the facilities are beginning to show their age.”"
}"]

["{

  "square reports more safety and trespassing concerns linked to neighborhood and campus access than circle": "Square repeatedly flags location and unauthorized access issues (\"The school is not located in a great area...random people who live nearby do come on campus...there are always police officers and staff outside, making sure no one enters the campus that shouldn't\"), while Circle does not describe trespassing or neighborhood-safety intrusions.",
  "square documents bullying and alleged misconduct by student resource officers while circle reports staff professionalism and student support instead": "Square alleges direct failures and misconduct (\"I have seen students bully other students in front of teachers and nothing has been done...The student resource officers sexually harass my friends by touching our shoulders\"), whereas Circle emphasizes attentive staff and supportive services (\"the staff, principal and teachers were attentive...Case manager and social worker are amazing!!!\").",
  "square reports inconsistent academic rigor and grade inflation for underprepared students while circle emphasizes consistent academic rigor and high expectations": "Square includes complaints that \"teachers passed\" students who \"couldn't even read\" and that the school is \"focused more on meeting the standards than actually caring about the education students are receiving,\" whereas Circle repeatedly praises rigorous programs and preparing students for college and STEM (\"The program is rigorous...Lane far better prepares its students for STEM education, college application, and life\").",
  "circle documents active investment in new physical infrastructure and program expansion while square reports aging or sub-par facilities and litter problems": "Circle mentions construction and program growth (\"there is currently a baseball stadium being built behind it!\" and many new course offerings), while Square complains about campus upkeep and facilities (\"We have a beautiful campus, but there is also a lot of trash everywhere...Facilities are sub-par\").",
  "square enforces visible ID-policy citations and lacks a dress code while circle describes no such disciplinary policy details": "Square describes specific on-campus policies and enforcement friction (\"Students are required to wear I.D.s. If you don't have your I.D. on you get a citation...There is no dress code and sometimes students come to school wearing pants that are too low\"), whereas Circle's reviews do not mention ID citation enforcement or an absence of dress code.",
  "circle reports clearer administrative responsiveness to individual student problems while square contains reports of adversarial or punitive administrative interactions": "Circle gives examples of administrators and teachers helping students recover when they struggle (\"When she had a problem last year, the staff, principal and teachers were attentive and have helped her get back on track\"), while Square contains parental complaints about punitive treatment and lack of advocacy (\"my children - who are honors students - are treated like criminals by the administration\")."

["{
  "circle has more personally caring and student focused teachers than square": "Circle states explicitly that \"The teachers really do care about all the students, ... really personally care about their well being,\" whereas Square complains staff are \"just very out of touch with students\" and describe a \"just doing my job -without regard for individual students-\" mindset.",

  "square attributes more school problems to community socioeconomic deprivation and underfunding than circle": "Square links problems to local poverty and funding shortfalls — \"Torrance county is littered w/ 'poor man's mentality'\" and \"NM has ZERO funding for education\" — while Circle only notes students are \"small town or farm kids\" without framing systemic poverty as the root cause.",

  "circle describes a test-heavy curriculum with scarce homework emphasis more than square": "Circle specifically criticizes the instructional balance: “What happened to giving children homework… instead constantly giving them tests back to back… Getting homework is rarely to none,” and “This school mostly focuses on tests and exams and put those higher above anything else.” Square’s curriculum complaints emphasize low rigor, multiple-choice tests, and retakes rather than the particular absence of homework.",

  "circle describes more proactive extracurricular programming and workshops than square": "Circle says the school \"has a lot to offer and so many different workshops,\" directly describing organized offerings, while Square's text focuses on problems within one program (band) and only scattered mentions of athletics/choir/technology without the same emphasis on organized workshops.",

  "square reports abusive or harassing staff behavior (especially in band) while circle reports staff who want to help students": "Square alleges the \"head band director often harasses students\" and that directors \"attempt to motivate the students ... by insult,\" whereas Circle states \"The teachers there are there for the students and really do want to help them,\" showing supportive staff behavior not described in Square.",
  "square reports specific neglect of student advancement opportunities in music (lack of encouragement for honor auditions) while circle does not report this problem": "Square says \"the directors don't encourage students to participate in honor band auditions\" and that only \"those who find out through private study under another teacher\" participate, indicating institutional neglect of advancement pathways; Circle does not mention barriers to extracurricular advancement.",

  "square reports wasted instructional time and staff apathy in classes while circle highlights engaged teachers": "Square describes teachers who \"act like they don't even want to be there; and to waste time instructors often talk whole class periods to avoid playing,\" indicating classroom time misuse; Circle emphasizes that \"teachers... really do want to help them,\" implying more engaged classroom practice.",
  "square documents program-level quality imbalance within band (strong marching, weak musicianship) while circle presents general program strengths without such imbalance": "Square states \"the marching itself is far superior to the way the group plays musically\" and calls marching \"the best it has been in history,\" pointing to uneven program quality; Circle generally asserts the school \"has a lot to offer\" without describing such internal program contradictions.",
  "circle reports explicitly structured student support and opportunities (workshops, teacher help) more than square": "Circle highlights concrete supports: \"a lot to offer and so many different workshops\" and teachers who \"really do want to help,\" whereas Square's reviews focus on problems (harassment, apathy, bullying) and note that students must rely on private teachers for some opportunities (\"private study under another teacher\")."

  "circle reports teachers expect self directed student responsibility more than square": "Circle says “Every teacher I've had is willing to help, but are waiting for the student to take responsibility in seeking the help” and describes Honors/AP as where “the student is expected to do the work themselves,” a theme of self‑directed expectations not emphasized in Square.",
  "square reports greater teacher availability and after school support than circle": "Square repeatedly notes teachers “are very willing to stay after school or come in early to help students” and that faculty “will go out of their way to support your child,” emphasizing active teacher time outside class, a practice Circle does not highlight.",

  "circle reports a student drug problem that administration fails to address whereas square does not mention drugs": "Circle warns “There is also a fairly good drug problem which the administration fails to address,” identifying a specific safety/discipline incident type that is not mentioned in Square.",

  "square provides concrete extracurricular participation metrics and program accolades whereas circle provides none": "Square gives a numeric participation detail (“over 15% of the school is involved” in marching unit) and names championship programs, while Circle provides no participation rates or comparable program accolades."

  "square reports frequent bullying and punitive discipline incidents whereas circle reports strong mutual respect": "Square details multiple bullying and discipline problems: \"The middle school teachers completely broke my son,\" \"My son was picked on and harassed by other students on a daily basis,\" and frequent suspensions for a student with autism; Circle emphasizes climate: \"The respect that the students and teachers share is incredible.\"",

  "square charges families many out of pocket fees whereas circle makes no mention of such charges": "Square lists extensive family costs: \"send your child with a lot of money... athletic fees, choir fees, band fees, club fees, paper, pens, tissues... snacks and drinks for the whole class to share,\" while Circle contains no complaints or mentions of extra fees.",
  "circle emphasizes an inductive environmental curriculum integrated with heavy academics whereas square includes no such curricular focus": "Circle explicitly states a distinctive pedagogy and theme: \"Don't be fooled by the name - yes, the curriculum does weave in environmental themes... the inductive learning environment is unique,\" whereas Square contains no references to environmental or inductive curriculum themes.",
  "circle reports stronger holistic student development outcomes (leadership, communication, self-understanding) than square": "Circle credits the school with nonacademic growth: \"helped him in communication skills, leadership, personal goal setting, and understanding himself and community,\" whereas Square's accounts focus on academic/administrative disputes, bullying, or test prep with little emphasis on these holistic outcomes.",
  "square depicts politicization of health and safety policies by governance whereas circle has no such politicization": "Square accuses the board of political interference in health policy: \"the board recently caved to far-right anti-vaxx/anti-maskers and refused to implement a mask mandate during a pandemic!\"; Circle includes no discussion of politicized health or board-level interference.",
  "square reports underfunded and deteriorating physical facilities more than circle": "Square includes facility complaints: \"Our sports centers are trashed, our buildings are falling apart at the seams, we have few resources,\" while Circle contains no references to poor facilities or resource shortages.",

  "circle diverts more staff time and resources to discipline and drug prevention at the expense of instruction than square": "Circle claims \"teachers and administrators are to[o] busy trying to limit drug use and maintain a safe environment that almost no resources are devoted to teaching,\" while Square highlights academic support and programs to prevent exclusion and bullying and emphasizes high academic expectations.",
  "circle shows greater teacher attrition and program collapse than square": "Circle reports that \"half the teachers left the school a few years ago\" and that leaders \"ran off some great teachers,\" producing program decline (\"The band has no competitions, no trips, and no more pride\"). Square mentions some teacher cuts and complaints but includes many positive statements about caring teachers and administrators.",
  "square demonstrates stronger advanced academic offerings and college readiness for some students than circle": "Square boasts that \"honors and AP classes are world-class\" and gives a concrete outcome: \"My oldest was definitely college ready at ASU... She’s in the engineering program and is a 4.0 student,\" while Circle notes \"There are only about 5 AP courses offered\" and a reviewer saying \"I do not think I was at all prepared for college.\"",
  "square supports broader and healthier extracurricular, performing arts, and athletic programs than circle": "Square lists multiple strong programs: \"Theater program and drama club are excellent,\" \"Their Performing Arts program is amazing!\" and \"my daughter plays volleyball and they have the best team in the state!\" In contrast, Circle describes decline in arts: the band and chorus \"used to have the best\" and now \"it is probably the worst\" with \"no competitions, no trips.\"",

    "square documents parental withdrawal of students to private school for safety while circle describes students remaining enrolled and succeeding": "Square states “I withdrew my two teenagers from this school and placed them in private schools,” showing parents removing children over safety/quality concerns; Circle is written by a current student who affirms students can succeed and remains enrolled.",

["{
  "circle enforces academic exclusion and barring of students for poor performance more than square": "Circle reviewers describe explicit removal/denial practices: “we just received the letter stating he would NOT be able to come back next year” and “a committee look at each student to determine if they meet 'McKeel criteria'” and “Get an F more than twice on your report card, and you get kicked out.” Square contains no description of school-level expulsions or systematic barring for grades.",
  "circle mandates costly required uniforms and difficult fitting logistics more than square": "Circle repeatedly details expensive, mandatory uniforms and burdensome fittings: “the uniform company... are over priced” and “if you transfer into the school, late in the year, you have to drive all the way to Clear-water to get a fitting.” Square includes no discussion of uniform mandates or associated costs/logistics.",
  "circle assigns heavier nightly homework and sustained out-of-school workload than square": "Circle reviewers report intense nightly work expectations: “You can expect about three and a half hours of homework a night” and “I'm working till 12 each night.. and I'm only in 8th grade.” Square mentions college prep and academic value but does not describe this level of nightly homework.",
  "circle exhibits more perceived socioeconomic and athletic favoritism affecting student treatment than square": "Circle claims institutional favoritism tied to wealth and varsity status: “If you are rich and can support the school financially you'll have no problem” and “if you help the school financially or are an important part of a varsity team then you get special treatment.” Square reports teacher favoritism (\"Teacher's play favourites\") and strong sports programs, but not systematic wealth-based or booster/varsity-linked preferential retention.",
  "square reports more responsive counseling and administrator intervention for bullying and crises than circle": "Square contains explicit claims of responsive student support: “vice principals or the guidance counselers will actually take time to talk with you and fix the problem immediately.” In contrast, Circle reviewers describe poor follow-up and denied requests: “several teachers will not return emails or phone calls” and “we asked to have our son moved to another teacher and were denied.”",
  "square provides explicit academic recovery programs and earlier college-preparatory supports more than circle": "Square explicitly cites programs to help failing students and early college preparation: “They help students prepare for college early. Also how they have something called a 'Credit Recovery' for students who fail a course one nine weeks.” Circle mentions strong academics and dual enrollment but contains no mention of credit-recovery programs aimed at keeping struggling students on track.",
  "circle reports more teacher aggression, yelling, and classroom harassment than square": "Circle describes teacher behavior that frightens students: “history teacher he was afraid of as a result of hero yelling in the class, telling them to shut up and more conduct that would be considered harassment in the work area.” Square more often describes teacher passivity or favoritism (\"teachers are afraid to do anything...\" and \"Teacher's play favourites\") rather than staff-initiated aggression.",
  "circle reports stronger technology resources than square": "Circle explicitly states greater tech resourcing: “They definitely are way more technologically advanced than most public school.” Square's reviews make no claims about superior technology or advanced digital resources.",
  "square enforces stricter restroom and passing-time policies that interfere with lunch and class breaks more than circle": "Square reviewers complain about restrictive daily-passage policies: “my teachers don't normally let anyone use the restroom during class... classes are so far apart that you do not have time between classes” and “during lunch they regulate how many people are in the restroom... sometimes you are standing in line not getting to eat your lunch.” Circle includes no accounts of such facility/time restrictions.",
  "circle prioritizes maintaining high school image and 'A' rating over supporting struggling students more than square": "Circle reviewers explicitly connect exclusion to image preservation: “it is for the image of the school so that they can weed out the so-so kids and have the best/rich kids to make sure that they continue to receive an 'A' school status” and “They really only seem to care about being an 'A' school.” Square emphasizes reputation and achievement but also describes remedial supports (credit recovery) and counseling interventions rather than image-driven weeding."
}"]

["{
  "circle shows more explicit technology and career pathways than square": "Circle lists concrete tech programs and career impact: reviewers cite 'Cyber Security team, Programming Team' and 'Mr. Archer has made me want to go into a computer career field' and say 'It also looks good on a resume for college and future jobs,' whereas Square's reviews focus on AP classes and general academics but do not describe school-run technology teams or explicit career-path programming.",

  "square exhibits socioeconomic-based entitlement and opportunity disparity more than circle": "Square explicitly claims 'parent's income determines student treatment' and describes students from an 'affluent area' with 'a sense of entitlement,' whereas Circle emphasizes a collaborative environment where 'every student strives for a good education' and describes the school as 'more of a family than just a class.'",
  "square shows less effective administrative leadership and inconsistent discipline than circle": "Square complains that 'The principal does not have strong leadership skills' and 'does not support the teachers' and later that a 'new principle... instated a strict dress code' and other inconsistent actions; Circle offers no such complaints and instead highlights teacher-led support and continuity.",
  "square reports more frequent student skipping and open campus attendance problems than circle": "Square repeatedly states 'kids are allowed to skip classes,' 'kids are allowed to come and go as they please,' and 'open campus,' and notes skipping 'compromises their learning,' while Circle contains no reports of pervasive skipping or open-campus attendance issues.",
