  "square describes classroom teachers abandoning instruction because of student behavior more than circle": "Square: “my teacher actually gave up teaching the class because no one would listen… Therefore, I ended up teaching myself out of the textbook,” a concrete report of instruction stopping due to behavior; Circle reports teacher removals for political/retaliatory reasons but not teachers quitting instruction because of day-to-day student behavior.",
  "circle reports tolerated nepotism in hiring and employment more than square": "Circle: “nepotism is tolarated in their employment system,” a direct accusation that hiring/employment favors relatives and influences staffing; Square contains no allegation of nepotism.",
  "circle reports administrators enforcing political agenda and rule oriented conformity more than square": "Circle: administrators are described as having “a conservative political agena” and being “oriented toward rule making and conformity rather than free thinking and learning,” indicating top-down political/rule focus; Square criticizes administration as unwelcoming to parents but does not describe political agendas or systematic conformity enforcement.",
  "circle reports serious failures in safety response to stalking incidents more than square": "Circle: “When a stalker was reported, nothing was done to protect me. I was told to carry a pocket knife and phone when walking places on campus,” a specific failure of safety policy and remedial protections; Square does not recount comparable failures to respond to stalking or targeted threats.",
  "circle reports neglect of special education programming more than square": "Circle: “My sibling was in special ed and they gave that group of kids nothing to do all day besides watch movies. The teachers in that department had no parent contact,” a specific claim of inadequate special education programming; Square does not mention special education shortcomings.",
  "circle reports higher teacher turnover and unstable leadership more than square": "Circle: “teacher turnover is high, and leadership isn't strong yet,” and multiple reviewers note administrative change and its effects; Square contains multiple positive remarks about staff stability and teachers being “wonderful” or “engaging,” with no mention of high turnover.",
  "square reports greater breadth of extracurricular options and AP availability than circle": "Square: “Guilford offered some good AP classes, such as AP biology… options available for students to be involved in sports, clubs and organizations,” whereas Circle explicitly states “we dont offer nearly as many extracurricular classes as we should” and “Few classes to choose from.”",
  "circle reports recent administrative changes that expanded career technical offerings more than square": "Circle: reviewers note improvements under new leadership, e.g. “They've done a great job of increasing the career tech offerings,” indicating active program expansion tied to administrative change; Square praises teachers and AP classes but contains no account of recent administrative-led expansion of career/technical programs.",
  "circle reports specific personnel retaliation driving out good teachers more than square": "Circle: “the school drove out one of the best teachers it had just because the superintendent was being controlled by the principal who had a personal vendetta against her,” an allegation of targeted retaliation affecting staffing; Square criticizes student behavior and teacher responses but does not describe targeted revenge-driven dismissal of teachers."
}"]

["{
  "circle shows more individualized curriculum adjustments and student-level acceleration than square": "Circle states clear individual tailoring: “Adjusted curriculum for my son to put him on advanced track” and “Ensured he is always challenged,” whereas Square contains no comparable claim of a teacher-initiated, one-on-one curriculum adjustment for a specific student.",
  "square shows more reported drug, crime, and safety problems inside the school than circle": "Square repeatedly alleges safety issues: “They have a terrible drug problem and crime is terrible,” “the crime is bad,” and “away from drugs,” while Circle contains no mention of drugs, crime, or safety concerns.",
  "square shows more parental attempts to withdraw children or actively leave the school than circle": "Square opens with and repeats removal efforts: “I am trying to get my kids out!,” “We are actively looking for a way out,” and “pulled my kid out as fast as i could,” whereas Circle expresses no intention to leave and instead praises the school.",
  "square shows greater within-school academic stratification and a bifurcated student culture (AP/preAP versus regular) than circle": "Square explicitly contrasts tracks: “This is a great school to be in if you take all AP classes... however, if you take regular classes, you get stuck with all the people that don't really care,” indicating a pronounced divide; Circle praises advanced placement for one child but does not describe an internal stratified culture.",
  "circle emphasizes stronger, consistent leadership and teacher engagement in students' academic growth than square": "Circle begins with “Outstanding school with extraordinary leadership” and claims “Teachers know each student and care about academic excellence,” presenting a coherent picture of engaged leadership and staff; Square contains mixed and contradictory statements about staff dedication rather than a consistent endorsement.",
  "square reports inconsistent teacher quality and alleges entrenched staff tolerance of bad behavior more than circle": "Square claims “I think it has some horrible teachers... it's the ones that have been there too long that set up the atmosphere for patting on the back of bad behavior ... drain the swamp,” pointing to uneven teacher quality and alleged long-term tolerance of misconduct; Circle offers only uniformly positive statements about teachers.",
  "square reports more negative peer influence, social isolation, and bullying experiences than circle": "Square describes social harm: “My child hated this school. He had very few friends and even the ones he did have were terrible to him” and notes peers as a source of drugs and distraction, while Circle emphasizes that the child “loves this school” socially and academically.",
  "square mentions concrete academic support programs, dual credit, and campus facility improvements more than circle": "Square notes “programs at the school to help bring up your child grade,” “I will be attending DICKINSON myself next year for a dual credit class,” and “Nice well maintained campus with many new facilities,” whereas Circle praises academics and sports but does not enumerate facilities upgrades or formal support programs.",
  "square documents notable college-level outcomes for some students despite its problems more than circle": "Square cites tangible student outcomes: “My sister graduated from DHS and will be attending the Business Honors program in the university of Texas at Austin” and “I plan on attending an Ivy League Institution,” evidence of successful college placements reported within the same school context; Circle praises advanced tracking but does not mention specific college outcomes.",
  "circle highlights sports programming as an explicitly positive aspect of student life more than square": "Circle states the student “loves this school both academically as well as the sports programs,” while Square makes no positive reference to sports programs or athletic offerings."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports far more failures in counseling and administrative responsiveness than square": "Circle repeatedly describes counselors and administrators as unresponsive and dysfunctional — e.g., “The counseling department is useless...they have too many students to serve!”, “If you send email or call they will not respond,” and “Her transcript was never sent...the dysfunctional counseling department did not sent the transcripts.” Square by contrast says staff are “open and available for the students.”",

  "circle shows more inconsistent and poor classroom instruction and teacher accountability than square": "Circle repeatedly accuses teachers of incompetence, poor pedagogy and lack of accountability — e.g., “MANY of the teachers are either incompetent, or pure lazy,” “team-taught math classes are very very poorly taught,” and “The ninth grade Math teacher is abysmal.” Square states teachers are “open and available” and gives positive one-on-one attention, indicating fewer instructional-quality complaints.",

  "circle reports more widespread classroom management and disruptive student behavior than square": "Circle describes classes where students socialize, phones and disruption are common and teachers cannot control classes — “the rest of the class is just sitting there socializing...,” “teachers couldn't keep the class under control,” and “students visably impared in the classroom.” Square emphasizes a small, close environment where “Everybody is kind and supportive,” suggesting less disruption.",

  "circle documents specific safety and drug issues ignored by staff whereas square does not": "Circle explicitly states “there is a horrible drug problem at this school and it is totally ignored by administration,” and multiple comments about students not feeling safe or being bullied; square has no mention of drugs or safety concerns and instead highlights kindness and support.",

  "circle reports inadequate special education and IEP support while square emphasizes one-on-one attention for all students": "Circle contains multiple reports of special needs being mishandled — “Do not service Special Education students satisfactorily,” “You'll never get it from the staff at JCHS,” and difficulty obtaining an IEP; square emphasizes small size yielding “more one on one time with their teachers,” implying better individualized support.",

  "circle reports systemic errors affecting student outcomes (college transcripts, AP availability) more than square": "Circle gives concrete examples of administrative mistakes harming outcomes — “her transcript was never sent...She paid the fee...but dysfunctional counseling department did not sent the transcripts,” and notes AP program constraints (“AP Program still in need - apparently budget constraints will not allow full offering”), whereas square makes no such claims about harmed outcomes.",

  "circle reports uneven and excessive student homework and workload pressure more than square": "Circle repeatedly complains students are “overworked,” e.g. “My son is doing homework all night,” “hours upon hours of it every single night,” and that middle-of-the-road students are overwhelmed; square does not describe heavy workload and instead highlights personalized attention.",

  "circle documents racial and social exclusion problems more than square": "Circle contains explicit allegations of minority students being bullied and a snobby, popularity-driven culture — “Minority (Asian, Black, and Hispanic) students are bullied,” “run by the popular kids and jocks...total snobs,” and “Majority of the students are ignorant and mean,” while square asserts that “Everybody is kind and supportive.”",

  "square presents a distinctly smaller, private-school–like environment and more consistent close-knit community than circle": "Square explicitly states “East Rochester feels like a private school due to the size...The small school environment gives students more one on one time,” while circle describes a larger comprehensive high school with many activities but repeatedly highlights impersonal bureaucracy and variability in teacher quality.",

  "circle reports inconsistent teacher-parent communication systems more than square": "Circle criticizes lack of a uniform communication method — “Some teachers use Edmodo, some use the hub, some use text and some use nothing,” and parents are left “sent in circles” — whereas square reports staff are “open and available,” implying reliable communication.",

  "circle highlights broad extracurricular and athletic scale but pairs it with administrative shortcomings unlike square": "Circle repeatedly praises the number of activities and strong sports programs (“The sports programs are great. The booster club...”), yet pairs those positives with recurring administrative and counseling failures; square emphasizes a small supportive community and does not emphasize a large extracurricular breadth."
}"]

    "square shows internal inconsistency about elective availability more than circle": "Within Square one reviewer complains electives were reduced by the 6 period day while another says \"there are many elective choices for students,\" indicating variability or uneven elective access across the student body or over time; Circle focuses on small-school attention rather than elective availability.",
    "circle exhibits more extreme polarized reviewer assessments of overall school quality than square": "Circle contains an extreme negative judgement alongside strong praise—\"This school rates a zero\" followed by \"I couldn't have been more pleased with their educational experience\"—presenting sharp disagreement about fundamental school quality that is more explicit than Square's mixed but less extreme statements."

["{
  "circle reports adult-to-student gossip and ethical breaches more than square": "Circle states that “grown adults gossip about children to other children” and calls this a moral/ethical failure, e.g. “It creates a toxic learning environment” caused by teacher-student gossip; square contains no comparable claim about adults gossiping about students.",
  "circle shows small-town staff/community entanglement and nepotism more than square": "Circle explicitly ties problems to local social networks: “This is a small town where everybody knows everybody … The teachers went here with many of the parents when they were in high school,” arguing that these ties drive favoritism; square includes outsider vs local tensions but not sustained claims of staff being alumni/relatives of families.",
  "circle describes teachers condoning or participating in student bullying more than square": "Circle alleges active teacher involvement in bullying: “students will gang up on someone and the teachers will ignore it or literally laugh along with them,” whereas square primarily reports administrative inaction or student-perpetrated incidents (e.g. a video of a beating) rather than teachers laughing or joining in.",
  "square reports institutional athletic prioritization (football over academics) more than circle": "Square repeatedly claims athletics dominate priorities: “West Monroe has consistently placed more emphasis on football than academics” and “places football over everything, including academics,” while circle makes no claim about a school-wide athletic overemphasis.",
  "square documents specific academic-policy practices that reduce rigor more than circle": "Square cites concrete policies and outcomes: “students with an A average are 'exempt'” from finals, “Only 3 or 4 students in an AP class of 20 actually took the AP test,” and grade-inflation examples where everyone who submitted a paper got an A; circle does not describe such formal academic exemption policies or AP/test participation data.",
  "square reports presence of high-quality specialized facilities and elite extracurricular programs more than circle": "Square highlights facilities and programs: “the new Science, Technology, Engineering and Math building was truly exceptional,” and music programs touring internationally (“choir will be in Italy … band just returned from London”), whereas circle contains no descriptions of exceptional facilities or elite program travel.",
  "square contains explicit allegations of racial incidents and mascot-related systemic racism more than circle": "Square recounts racial incidents and contested symbols: cheerleaders saying they have to lock doors because they were in “niggerville,” and criticism of the school mascot being the “rebels” tied to the Confederacy; circle has no mention of race-related incidents or mascot controversies.",
  "circle emphasizes rumor-based allegations about administrative misconduct while square cites concrete, documentable incidents": "Circle foregrounds hearsay: “disturbing rumors about the principal are whispered by parents, students and even teachers” and that the principal “was moved from another school because he had problems,” while square names tangible incidents with traceable evidence—recorded videos, reported assaults, AP test participation counts and a recorded cheerleader comment—rather than primarily anonymous whispers.",
  "square shows highly polarized simultaneous experiences (strong praise and strong criticism) more than circle": "Square contains both multiple glowing accounts of elite academics and programs (“My children graduated … are proud alumni,” “world class educational standards,” exceptional STEM building) and severe criticisms (racism, beaten student video, grade inflation), producing starkly conflicting portrayals; circle’s reviews are far more consistently negative about administration, favoritism and ethics."
}"]

["{
  "square documents frequent bullying and social harassment while circle does not": "Square contains multiple reports of peer mistreatment and exclusion (“people spread stuff about you,” “my friend was constantly taunted about her looks,” “bullying does exist”), whereas Circle contains only a neutral observational sentence and no mention of bullying.",
  "square reports school officials overlooking student harassment whereas circle does not": "Square explicitly states an administrative failure to intervene: “The school officials just over look them,” describing staff inaction around taunting; Circle contains no description of staff overlooking incidents.",
  "square describes high academic rigor and prevalence of Honors/AP courses while circle does not": "Square details challenging coursework and advanced offerings: “My classes at Central were often times more challenging than freshman and sophomore level college classes,” and “Most students take at least one honors or AP class,” while Circle has no mention of course rigor or advanced programs.",
  "square details multi-level tracking and manipulation of course levels unlike circle": "Square describes an explicit leveling system and policy changes: “There are 4 levels of classes… the administration pushed many students from regular level classes up into Honors level, but then removed much of the Honors content,” whereas Circle gives no information about class structure or tracking.",
  "square reports concrete administrative policy conflicts and equity-driven curricular changes while circle does not": "Square references board division and an administration pursuing an ‘equal outcomes’ agenda that reduces content and changes grading: “The Board of Education is also sharply divided… discontinue top quality academics with the social objective of achieving 'equal outcomes'… Many classes also no longer count homework,” while Circle contains no policy-level descriptions.",
  "square notes declining enrollment and falling test scores attributable to policies while circle does not": "Square links administrative changes to measurable outcomes: “enrollment is now declining and so are test scores as stunned families increasingly abandon ship,” whereas Circle includes no outcome data or enrollment information.",
  "square reports strong college-preparation supports and counselor involvement whereas circle does not": "Square explicitly praises college counseling and outcomes: “The guidance counselors are excellent… Students leave well prepared for college,” and cites where graduates matriculate, while Circle provides no information about college prep or counselor roles.",
  "square describes substantial extracurricular and athletic breadth while circle does not": "Square highlights a wide array of activities: “There are hundreds of sport and extracurricular activities and clubs for all types of interests” and emphasizes athletics and personal development, while Circle mentions neither clubs nor athletics.",
  "square documents concerns about racial composition and minority students feeling out of place while circle does not": "Square discusses demographics and perceived race-related exclusion: “Hinsdale is predominately white and non-Caucasian students may feel out of place,” and notes diversity trends, whereas Circle has no discussion of racial makeup or inclusion.",
  "square reports facilities shortcomings despite academic reputation while circle does not": "Square warns that physical infrastructure is lacking: “Facilities are substandard, but don't be fooled,” juxtaposing facilities with reputation; Circle only states “Beautiful school” and does not report facility problems.",
  "square reports active debate and negative effects of grading and homework policy changes while circle does not": "Square alleges concrete grading-policy changes tied to equity (“Many classes also no longer count homework toward a student's grade because that would be unfair”) and discusses the consequences, while Circle contains no description of grading or homework policies.",
  "square describes socioeconomic cliques and ostracism based on wealth or feeder schools while circle does not": "Square describes social stratification: “If you are not very well off or went to Westview Hills Middle School you are considered scum and feel very left out,” indicating socioeconomic/external-school based exclusion, which Circle does not mention.",
  "circle reports visible positive physical appearance and direct teacher-student interaction while square does not emphasize that observation": "Circle gives a concrete visual appraisal—“Beautiful school and teacher is teaching a student”—focusing on aesthetics and a live classroom scene, whereas Square focuses on systemic programs, policies, and outcomes rather than a simple onsite description."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports more severe physical violence and visible injury incidents than square": "Circle contains graphic accounts of physical assaults and blood — e.g. “If you want your kid to see a school administrator get beat up... blood on the walls after a fight...” — whereas Square only describes bullying and harassment without graphic physical-violence detail (“a lot of bullying that doesn't get handled properly”).",
  "square reports a pronounced lack of racial/ethnic diversity while circle describes exposure to and learning from diversity": "Square states bluntly “there is absolutely NO diversity” and warns ‘unless ur preppy and white, good luck,’ whereas Circle includes statements like “This school made me become a very open person to diversity and differences” and contrasts itself to a ‘suburban whitewashed school.’",
  "circle describes more unresponsive or hostile guidance and administrative behavior than square": "Multiple Circle passages complain about guidance/admin attitudes and inaction: “the guidance counselor… had the worst attitude… wanted to get off the phone” and “guidance counselors didn't care and would give the students useless classes,” while Square explicitly praises support staff: “awesome high school guidance staff.”",
  "circle records direct accusations of abusive or negligent security/staff behavior more than square": "Circle alleges physical harm and impunity by staff: “bad security guards which i was previously injured by 1 of them Mr Leeland whom was never fired,” and recounts administrators being attacked or ineffective; Square mentions bullying and cover-ups but does not report staff-caused physical injuries.",
  "circle gives more concrete descriptions of vocational, technical, and elective offerings than square": "Circle lists specific courses and programs (e.g. “Psychology, Graphic tech and woodshop,” “photography, desktop publishing, psychology, and biomedical science,” and laments losing an automotive program), whereas Square only generically cites “Excellent sports and music programs” and “a plethora of opportunities” without detailed program names.",
  "square alleges institutional cover-ups of problems whereas circle focuses on administrative neglect and systemic causes": "Square explicitly accuses the school of concealment: “they have so many issues that get covered up,” while Circle frames failures as administrative neglect and structural causes: “it's the administration and the overall poverty of some of these cities” and criticizes policies like No Child Left Behind.",
  "square reports a higher stated prevalence of student drug use than circle": "Square claims a specific high prevalence: “a good 80% of the students do drugs,” while Circle mentions drug paraphernalia incidents and students “trying to make bongs and pipes” but does not claim such a broad prevalence percentage.",
  "circle reports specific academic placement problems that threaten graduation more than square": "Circle contains warnings that counselors give “useless classes that could cost them the ability to graduate” and parents saying classes were being picked for their child without proper consultation, whereas Square praises guidance and resources and does not report placement-to-graduation risks.",
  "circle invokes community socioeconomic and policy-level explanations for school problems more than square": "Circle attributes some poor outcomes to external factors: “the overall poverty of some of these cities, like Milwaukee” and “No Child Left Behind has a lot to do with the bad test scores,” a context absent from Square’s descriptions.",
  "square emphasizes stronger district-level reputation and school spirit than circle": "Square contains positive claims of district quality and pride: “Exeter Senior High School is the culmination of the excellent education offered by all of the Exeter township schools,” “Much better than surrounding area school districts,” and “impressive school spirit,” while Circle contains more accounts of institutional failure and safety concerns despite a few comments about building character.",
  "square portrays teachers as more consistently dedicated while circle contains mixed claims about teacher care and competence": "Square asserts “Most teachers are dedicated” and “Excellent education,” whereas Circle contains conflicting accounts — accusations that “teachers cant teach” and that “a good deal of them didn't care” alongside other reviewers saying “the teachers here were more than amazing,” indicating less consistency in reported teacher commitment."
}"]

  "square reports strong, department-level academic rigor and college-prep outcomes more than circle": "Square includes specific praise for academic rigor and college readiness: '11th grade Honors English teacher was phenomenal... it prepared me for college,' and 'All of the English teachers I had were great... history teachers... influential,' whereas Circle offers no comparable department-level praise and focuses on overall instructional failures.",
  "square reports security incidents, threats, and surveillance/camera failures more than circle": "Square mentions 'threats to a school shooting over social media,' 'lots of drugs at Thomas Dale,' and a car break-in where they 'couldn't pull up the tapes,' implying camera or recording failures; Circle does not report such safety incidents or surveillance failures.",
  "square shows heterogeneous teacher quality with multiple explicit praises, whereas circle portrays predominantly uniformly negligent teachers": "Square contains many testimonials praising specific teachers and departments ('Honors English teacher was phenomenal,' 'All of the English teachers I had were great,' 'We have enjoyed the amazing arts programs'), while also criticizing some teachers, demonstrating variability; Circle mainly levels broad accusations that 'The teachers are lazy' and 'they don't care,' giving a more uniformly negative picture of teacher quality.",
  "circle highlights a positive JROTC program presence while square does not mention JROTC": "Circle names JROTC as 'the only good part in CHS' and praises program leaders ('Go Sgt and Col !!'), a specific extracurricular program that Square's reviews do not reference.",
  "square reports parking, entrance and exit safety hazards associated with overcrowding more than circle": "Square specifically warns 'parking, entrance and exiting the school is dangerous' and links it to overcrowding and two campuses, a logistical safety concern not raised in Circle.",
  "circle depicts district-level systemic decline and risk of state takeover more than square": "Circle contains district-level diagnoses such as 'This district is a sinking ship, and will most likely be taken over by the state within a few years,' a claim about systemic administrative failure beyond a single school that Square's reviews do not make.",
  "square reports perceived preferential treatment of arts students leaving non-arts students feeling ignored more than circle": "Square reviewers allege that 'If you're not in the arts program it seems as though you're just another number' and 'your child is only acknowledged or known if he/she is in the \"arts\" program or a \"trouble maker,\"' indicating perceived favoritism tied to program enrollment not present in Circle."

  "square reports broad advanced academic offerings, many academic clubs, and up to date technology more than circle": "Square: “They offer a variety of honor and AP courses… many academic clubs… Clean and up to date with technology,” describing concrete curricular breadth and resources; Circle does not describe extensive AP/honors offerings or technology resources and even notes gaps in gifted programming."

["{
  "circle provides more successful IEP mainstreaming support than square": "Circle explicitly states, “My son has an IEP and Conrad has helped him mainstream into the rest of the school with no problems at all,” indicating concrete special-education inclusion; Square contains no comparable descriptions of effective IEP integration or inclusion support.",
  "circle shows more upward movement into Honors/AP classes than square": "Circle recounts teachers who “moved him from CP in math and english to Honors and he will now be AP level,” and cites high standardized and AP scores; Square repeatedly complains about weak college placement and lower top-tier college acceptance, with no evidence of routine upward academic tracking.",
  "circle reports more organized and responsive school leadership than square": "Circle: “The Principal is very organized and communicates well.” In contrast, Square includes multiple complaints about unresponsive or ineffective leadership and district offices, e.g., “Bregy never responded,” “need some smart, experienced, and caring leadership FAST,” and calls to fire the principal.",
  "circle reports better maintained, cleaner facilities than square": "Circle claims the building is “very nice and clean,” while Square repeatedly documents physical decline: “buildings need a facelift,” “campus is run down and dirty,” “pest problems,” and “textbooks are so old they disintegrate.”",
  "circle describes friendlier older-student mentorship and stronger community cohesion than square": "Circle says “even the older kids are very friendly and helpful to us (six graders)” and “offers a strong community sense,” whereas Square notes weak school pride, low extracurricular involvement, and a “too cool for school” attitude that reduces community engagement.",
  "circle portrays more consistently engaged and nurturing teachers while square reports more inconsistent and sometimes abusive or uncaring teachers": "Circle praises teachers and a named teacher’s interactive practices (“Mr.Olesky throws parties…we also play games”), and thanks “each and every one of his teachers and coaches”; Square catalogs numerous accounts of disengaged or abusive teachers, e.g., “terribly horrible Algebra teacher,” “teachers barely engage their students,” and “some gifted teachers have been let go, and abusive teachers allowed to stay on.”",
  "circle reports stronger measurable academic outcomes and college preparedness than square": "Circle notes “His standardized test… are high, his AP test scores are high” and that the student “will be prepared to move on to college,” while Square states “acceptance rate of students by top tier colleges is not as high” and that “one-third of the graduating class will be going to a community college.”",
  "square documents more prevalent student substance use (vaping) and lax enforcement than circle": "Square reports: “Almost every time I go into the bathroom there is a group of students vaping” and notes little consequence, whereas Circle contains no reports of vaping, drugs, or similar substance issues.",
  "square reports more pronounced ethnic clustering and limited student diversity leading to prejudice than circle": "Square explicitly says the student body is “predominantly Persian and Jewish” and that students “develop prejudices,” whereas Circle offers no parallel reports of ethnic clustering or race-based prejudice and includes multilingual/Spanish praise (“Excelente escuela…”).",
  "square shows weaker counseling and college-guidance capacity than circle": "Square describes overloaded counselors (“many of them have 200 or more students”), calls for improved college counseling, and gives examples of students defaulting to community college; Circle reports staff that monitor placement into Honors/AP and expresses confidence students “will be prepared to move on to college.”",
  "square indicates an administrative focus on residency policing and student exclusion that circle does not document": "Square describes a “District culture of sifting out students using claims of non residency” and threats to co‑custody students, while Circle describes stability for students who have been in the feeder pattern and no similar exclusions.",
  "square reports older facilities and outdated instructional materials whereas circle reports current rigor and classroom engagement practices": "Square: “textbooks are so old they disintegrate… there is nothing educationally cutting-edge,” while Circle cites active classroom practices and rigor (games like 24 in pre-algebra, moving students to Honors/AP) and parents praising the school’s rigor and high test/AP scores.",
  "square describes an environment where athletics are prioritized over academics more than circle": "Square repeatedly claims the school is “slanted more towards athletics than academics” and criticizes bell schedules and priorities, whereas Circle emphasizes rigorous academics, AP/Honors advancement, and academic achievement with only a brief note asking to update sports listings."
}"]

["{
  "square credits named principal leadership and school improvement more than circle": "Square explicitly credits a named leader: “This progress is because of Mr. Perry's, principal of Bellflower High, outstanding leadership and determination,” framing recent school improvement as leadership-driven; Circle contains no comparable praise of central leadership or named administrators.",
  "square reports stronger college outcomes and academic aspiration more than circle": "Square claims upward mobility and college placement: “A student from BHS can go to UCLA, Stanford, CalTech, UC Berkeley, etc.” and notes alumni and current students attending universities, whereas Circle contains no statements about college matriculation or academic advancement.",
  "circle reports severe facility problems and deferred maintenance more than square": "Circle documents concrete facility failures: “they dont hardly clean… worry about sports when the roof despertly needs to be redone” and gym closure due to infestation, while Square does not describe similar structural or maintenance crises.",
  "circle reports pest infestation and cleanliness failures more than square": "Circle explicitly reports rats and poor cleaning: “Last year we couldent go in the gym because there were rats and they were all over the school,” a specific sanitation/pest problem absent from Square.",
  "circle describes frequent teacher turnover and staffing instability more than square": "Circle recounts teacher churn: “We went threw 4 math teachers until the found one to stay,” indicating unstable staffing; Square discusses teachers positively but gives no examples of repeated turnover.",
  "circle reports excessive teacher workload and limited planning time more than square": "Circle mentions teacher assignment pressure: “Teacher workload is a way too much. (6 classes/one planning period),” indicating structural workload problems not described in Square.",
  "circle documents unequal resource allocation and prioritization more than square": "Circle highlights perceived misprioritization and resource inequity: “They will supply the freshman and sophmores with chromebooks (but not the juniors and seniors) and worry about sports when the roof desperately needs to be redone,” whereas Square does not report such allocation disputes.",
  "circle reports neglect of low performing students and selective support more than square": "Circle states a pattern of selective assistance: “This school only helps the best students and leave the others behind,” describing an explicit practice of prioritizing high performers while neglecting others; Square emphasizes broad teacher dedication and support for students.",
  "circle reports frequent classroom disruptions and unmanaged student behavior more than square": "Circle lists in-class interruptions and behavior problems: “Too much disruptions during teaching time, phone calls, students’ walk-ins etc.” and “The school has too many slackers… They just come to class to play video games,” while Square focuses on improvement and student success rather than pervasive classroom disorder.",
  "circle documents counseling staff inattentiveness and unprofessional behavior more than square": "Circle gives a specific incident of counselor disengagement: “she was checking her facebook on her smartphone and checking personal emails… I did not contact her anymore,” whereas Square explicitly says “Counselors are great,” showing the opposite pattern.",
  "square documents alumni and multi generation positive experiences more than circle": "Square includes multiple retrospective endorsements from former students and parents: “I attended Bellflower High School… If i could turn back time, I would,” and “My two eldest children graduated… had nothing but the best experiences,” a theme absent from Circle.",
  "square encourages parent community involvement and shared responsibility more than circle": "Square explicitly urges parental engagement and shared responsibility: “Attend your school meetings… It takes a village to raise a child… Motivate your children and teach them respect,” while Circle contains no call for parent collaboration and instead reports disengaged staff and unmet student needs."
}"]

  "circle shows lax enforcement of classroom rules and permissive cell phone use more than square": "Circle states \"Cell phones allowed and used in the classrooms by the kids, but not for school related things,\" indicating permissive policy and poor enforcement; Square has no comments about enforcement of classroom rules or phone policies.",
  "circle reports concrete curricular and academic quality problems more than square": "Circle asserts that \"the english departments curriculum\" needs improvement and that \"the quality of the education is tremendously lacking,\" while Square focuses on material and staffing needs (\"They need supplies and other learning materials\") rather than explicit curriculum or instruction failures.",

  "circle reports counseling staff failing to advocate for students more than square": "Circle warns \"Beware of the counselors, they are lazy and will fail to accommodate your children's needs unless you vocalize and make said demands,\" while Square does not mention counseling services or responsiveness.",

["{
  "circle emphasizes Catholic identity and mission more than square": "Circle repeatedly identifies the school as a Catholic institution and refers to mission and Catholic teaching: e.g., “Bourgade Catholic,” “It follows Catholic teaching(for the most part),” “BCHS really does fulfill their Mission!”; Square contains no references to religion or religious mission.",
  "circle reports a small, family-like community and close interpersonal familiarity more than square": "Multiple circle reviewers describe a “family-like feel,” knowing “nearly everyone at the school by name,” and a “small community” where students don’t get lost; Square mentions strong staff and new facilities but does not describe a pervasive small, family-style community.",
  "square reports recent capital investment in campus facilities, arts budget, and technology more than circle": "Square reviewers note a “new campus,” “high school auditorium,” “a lot of new technology available to the students,” and an active arts budget; circle reviews focus on culture, alumni and college prep and do not reference new facilities or major capital upgrades.",
  "circle reports multi-generational alumni involvement and long-term family ties more than square": "Circle includes several family-generation claims: “Our children are 3rd generation to Bourgade - my spouse and I are alumni as well as my parents!” and repeated alumni pride; Square offers no similar evidence of multi-generational family/alumni continuity.",
  "square reports specific, ongoing cafeteria food quality and food-safety problems more than circle": "Square contains detailed complaints about lunches — “Chunky mashed potatoes, yellow pepperoni,” “COLD chicken, pink burgers,” and allergy risk from unexpected whole wheat pizza — whereas circle contains no comments about lunch food or cafeteria safety.",
  "circle presents a stronger, explicit emphasis on college-preparatory outcomes and college admissions confidence than square": "Circle repeatedly asserts college-prep success and confidence in admissions and scholarships: “especially it being a College Prep school,” “I have no doubt my son and my daughter will get into the college of their choice and scholarship funds as well,” while Square only briefly notes that “colleges seem to accept these students readily.”",
  "circle describes easier, broader student access to extracurriculars and multiple sports participation because of low competition more than square": "Circle explicitly promotes low internal competition enabling involvement: “the school is at such a low competition rate that it's easy to play multiple sports guaranteed and join tons of different clubs,” while Square mentions strong sports programs but does not claim low competition or unusually broad access.",
  "square documents bullying problems and ineffective anti-bullying implementation more than circle": "Square contains strong statements that bullying is poorly handled despite programs: “the school has done POORLY at handling bullying, even with the new Olweus program,” and that staff don’t help sufficiently; circle mentions “troubles that roam among the students” but lacks specific reports of systemic bullying policy failure.",
  "square reports uneven teaching quality with many reviewers calling a majority of teachers ineffective more than circle": "A Square reviewer claims “The majority are poor” and that many “can't teach well at all,” while Circle reviewers more often describe teachers as “kind and welcoming,” “prepared him for college,” and generally supportive, with only isolated teacher-quality complaints.",
  "square reports curriculum maintenance problems and piecemeal academic updates more than circle": "Square reviewers state “The curriculum does need to be updated; the most recent updates have been piecemeal,” and criticize senior project priorities, whereas Circle focuses on college prep and does not raise curriculum-update or coherence concerns.",
  "circle reports administrative decision-making that reduces parent/student voice and community influence more than square": "Circle explicitly accuses administration of centralizing control and excluding others: “The administration makes most of the decisions and many parents and students have a problem with it because they generally have no say in it,” while Square’s administration criticisms center on leadership turnover, promises not delivered, and lack of help for nonconforming students rather than top-down exclusion of community voice.",
  "square reports leadership turnover and unmet administrative promises impacting nonconforming students more than circle": "Square highlights principal leadership failures and unfulfilled commitments to students who “didn't 'fit in the box'”: “The new principal has promised more than he has delivered so far,” and parents of non-cookie-cutter students report little help, a dynamic not described in Circle."
}"]

  "circle reports arbitrary unwritten policies and selective enforcement tied to favoritism more than square": "Circle describes ad hoc rules imposed by staff that apply selectively: \"On occasion, the principal or a random office employee, will declare a new rule or policy (not written in the student handbook) which only certain students must abide by,\" implying systemic selective enforcement; Square mentions isolated strict enforcement (e.g., CSI for a logo) but lacks Circle's pattern of unwritten, connection-driven policy imposition.",
  "square contains multiple insider endorsements (alumni, parents, teachers) documenting school strengths more than circle": "Square includes praise from diverse insiders—\"I graduated in 2010...I made it to an Ivy League school,\" \"I have been teaching at Varela since the school opened...Varela is definetly one of the best High Schools in Miami,\" and parent testimonials about magnet success—while Circle's reviewers are overwhelmingly critical with only brief concessions to a \"FEW good teachers.\"",
  "circle emphasizes misuse of adult authority in classrooms (yelling, power misuse) while square emphasizes higher instructional quality in advanced courses": "Circle criticizes teacher conduct: \"I believe teachers should not yell at children...It teaches inappropriate use of power,\" and complains about staff behavior broadly; Square highlights instructional strength in advanced coursework: \"most of the AP courses are absolutely wonderful, the teachers really know what they are teaching,\" showing a contrast between reported classroom culture and instructional rigor."

["{
  "circle shows stronger wealth-based social stratification and materialism than square": "Circle repeatedly links belonging to family wealth and visible displays of wealth to social status: \"If you don't have money and I mean lots of Money your kid will not fit into the Peer groups...The kids compete socially by seeing who can drive the most expensive car to school.\" Square by contrast highlights socioeconomic diversity and explicitly says \"no one feels judged\" and observes a relaxed environment.",
  "circle reports more athletic favoritism centered on football and athlete academic leniency than square": "Circle complains \"The athletics are all based around football...The football players are also put on a pedestal and their academic infractions are almost always overlooked,\" while square mentions successful sports programs but frames concerns as \"volatile directors and coaches\" and lax discipline generally rather than a single-sport pedestal.",
  "circle documents observed student drug use and related concerns while square does not": "Circle includes a direct parental observation: \"My child saw a lot of drug usage as well.\" Square contains no comparable mention of student drug use in its reviews.",
  "circle emphasizes visible college-prep programs (IB, career services, College Corps) and related prestige more than square": "Circle repeatedly cites specialized college-prep offerings and outcomes: \"Highly acclaimed IB program...It has a great career services center...It offers College Corps program for graduating students,\" whereas square focuses on the Cambridge program but has a mix of praise and complaints rather than the repeated institutional praise seen in circle.",
  "square reports more chronic infrastructure and overcrowding problems than circle": "Square describes facility issues impacting safety and comfort: \"overcrowded, almost to the point of danger...classrooms without AC, sub par labs and overall pitiful infrastructure,\" while circle mentions \"great facilities\" and does not report systemic overcrowding or building-condition problems.",
  "square reports more administrative unresponsiveness and failure to act on parent concerns than circle": "Square includes multiple statements about administration giving \"lip service\" and not taking action: \"The biggest negative is the administration and lack of support...lip service is given but no real action gets taken,\" whereas circle contains both criticism of impersonality but also explicit praise for caring administrators: \"Principal Hechtman truly cares\" and \"teachers and administrators are a dedicated group.\"",
  "square reports specific disciplinary bias in enforcement (dress code targeting females and disciplinary targeting of Black students) more explicitly than circle": "Square accuses the school of selectively enforcing rules: \"calling out only women for dress code, and only blacks for trouble making,\" and gives details about dress code policing; circle describes social hostility toward minorities but frames it as peer cliquishness and exclusion rather than procedural bias in official enforcement.",
  "circle reports widespread student academic struggle and students feeling unprepared for college despite rigorous coursework more than square": "Circle contains repeated first-person claims of academic struggle and being unprepared: \"I could say truthfully that I struggle in every class...I am a junior at Washington State this year, and i did not feel prepared for college.\" Square presents a mixed picture of Cambridge classes being \"challenging but not overwhelming\" with parents praising college preparation in some cases.",
  "square highlights successful, organized extracurricular programs and after-school academic supports more than circle": "Square names strong, organized programs and supports: \"The band and sports programs are highly successful...there's a great tutoring program run by the teachers in the library after school that's very helpful,\" while circle's extracurricular comments focus on athletics domination by football and only occasional praise for clubs or IB extracurriculars.",
  "circle reports parents transferring students out because of social climate more than square": "Circle explicitly states a parental transfer decision tied to social environment: \"I finally had to transfer my child to another high shool because of it.\" Square contains complaints about administration and program quality but does not include explicit reports of parents transferring children for social climate reasons."
}"]

["{

  "square references active district leadership and community pride while circle does not": "Square credits district-level leadership and community cohesion: “The superintendent ... has made many positive contributions to Burnet school system” and “we are a solid community who takes pride in our town and schools,” indicating administrative involvement and community support absent from Circle.",

["{
  "circle has stronger academic rigor and college-prep focus than square": "Circle repeatedly describes a rigorous, college-preparatory curriculum and strong academic outcomes: reviewers cite high ACT/SAT scores (“He scored very, very well on his ACTs and SATs”), “curriculum is rigorous,” and statements like “First rate education” and “prepare you well for demanding college coursework.” Square describes weak/mediocre academics and even says “A complete tragedy of a school system” and “I would NOT recommend it for any family,” with only “The education program is okay” at best.",
  
  "circle provides formal college counseling resources at a higher level than square": "Circle explicitly lists extensive college counseling infrastructure: “There are 4 full time college counselors and 6 part time… they visit 72 campuses a year,” whereas Square contains no mention of structured college counseling and focuses on local K–12 reconfiguration and budget issues rather than college-prep supports.",
  
  "circle shows less institutional support for students with learning or behavioral disorders than square": "Multiple circle reviews warn that the school is a ‘sink-or-swim’ environment with ‘no services for kids like this’ and personal testimony: “I have Asperger's… The administration sat passively… I personally do not recommend that school for anyone especially those with intellectual disabilities.” Square does report slow/inadequate follow-through but documents at least some eventual intervention after parent initiation: “school did nothing but drag their feet on follow through and putting together a plan (at my initiation, NOT theirs).”",
  
  "square reports more disruptive distraction from school-issued laptops than circle": "Square states plainly that district-issued MacBooks “has proven to be NOTHING but a distraction to the children.” Circle mentions iPads as part of broader change (“Between the iPads... failing cover up”) but does not emphasize them as the primary source of classroom distraction the way Square does.",
  
  "square experienced budget-driven grade consolidation and reconfiguration while circle does not": "Square details concrete reorganization: “K-2 are together in one building… they combined 4th-7th in the middle school and put the 8th graders in the highschool” and attributes it to “low attendance” and “budget cuts.” Circle’s reviews describe stable grade structure and do not report such consolidation.",
  
  "square reports poorer coaching quality and limited athletic scouting than circle": "Square accuses coaches of sticking to favorites and poor strategy: “coaches are just ridiculous and stick with favorites… football coach makes the same plays every damn time” and “there is no recruiting for sports.” Circle mentions sports and some positive athletic outcomes (alumni playing hockey/baseball, one attending Georgetown) and frames athletics as part of robust extracurriculars rather than chronically inept coaching.",
  
  "circle offers broader and more developed extracurricular and service programs than square": "Circle repeatedly lists many extracurricular strengths—service, theater, debate, clubs, sports—and community ethos: “Service and the spirit of doing good for others is at the heart of the school,” “plenty of clubs, activities and sports.” Square focuses on limited community amenities and complains “There is nothing for the kids to do,” aside from noting a new elementary building.",

  "square reports worse lunch quality and explicit complaints about meal portions and pricing than circle": "Square criticizes food directly: “inflated lunch prices,” “School lunch is absolutely disgusting… Growing teenagers need more then just a snack for lunch.” Circle mentions that attending is “quite expensive to attend, even the food” but does not provide the same detail about poor portions or disgust.",
  
  "circle includes accounts of highly credentialed teachers and specialized staff more than square": "Circle reviewers name high qualifications among staff—“I have worked with a Harvard valedictorian and an astrophysicist with a Stanford PhD,” “staff at this school are some of the rudest individuals I have ever met” (mixed)—and emphasize specialized college counselors. ["{
  "circle describes a small, close knit school community and individualized attention more than square": "Circle reviewers explicitly call it small and intimate: “Eldred is a small school where the kids all know each other… your child is not a number… administration is approachable and the teachers are very focused and recognize the specific needs of each student… Its like getting a private school for free!!” Square instead repeatedly describes large passing-period crowds, low parent participation, and overwhelmed counselors rather than one-on-one attention.",

  "square describes large student population crowding and poor hallway monitoring more than circle": "Square reviews tell readers to “Take a tour of the school during a period change and you will see” and state “The students aren't adequately monitored in the hallways, which aids in the bullying,” and observers note suspicious, gang-like groups during passing periods; circle contains no descriptions of crowding or inadequate hallway monitoring and emphasizes small size.",

  "square documents broader advanced academic and college-preparation programs more than circle": "Square mentions explicit programmatic advantages: “K level and AP classes,” “National Honor Society,” “incredible College Academy program,” and a reviewer credits the school’s career preparation for later success in engineering, while circle’s reviews do not describe AP, honors, or formal college-prep programs.",

  "square reports counselor shortages and staff overwork more than circle": "Square directly states “Counselors care but they are overworked… school district needs more counselors at this school,” indicating a staffing constraint for student support; circle reviews make no mention of counselor capacity or overload.",

  "circle reports administrative nonresponsiveness to bullying and failure to communicate discipline (hazing) more than square": "Circle explicitly accuses staff of inaction: “This school is lax, and non responsive to bullying,” and recounts that when the football team was allegedly suspended for hazing administrators “failed to inform the public… I was given days of run around, with the bullies faring no consequences.” Square also reports bullying but includes statements about discipline and security (see below) rather than this specific pattern of noncommunication about athletic discipline.",

  "square reports racial demographic dominance and racially motivated bullying and suggests rezoning more than circle": "Square contains repeated claims linking majority-race domination to daily issues: “When one race dominates the demographics of a school, there are bound to be issues… THIS IS AN ISSUE EVERY DAY HERE… My children whom are white-Hispanic, have been bullied and or scared by students who are racially prejudiced… HOW ABOUT REZONING?,” whereas circle’s bullying descriptions do not frame problems as schoolwide racial-demographic conflict.",

  "circle reports athletic hazing incidents affecting multiple teams and opaque consequences more than square": "Circle recounts a hazing-related athletics incident where a football suspension was mishandled and teams share members so discipline had wider impact: “When their football team was allegedly suspended…and therefore, technically were still able to participate in sports… I was given days of run around,” while square criticizes emphasis on sports (‘Ram Pride’) but does not report a specific hazing incident or failure to communicate athletic discipline.",

  "square connects classroom instruction breakdown to student disruptions more than circle": "Multiple square reviewers say students “dominating this school” cause teachers to be unable to teach and thus “resort to assigning homework and not really TEACHING very much in class,” explicitly attributing instructional loss to behavioral disruption; circle’s instructional complaints focus on teachers not explaining new topics rather than on student-driven classroom disruption.",

  "square documents on-campus security presence and active monitoring for skipping more than circle": "Square notes “we have cops and teachers who keep that on check which is good!!” in the context of skipping and supervision; circle contains no mention of law enforcement, campus police, or formal monitoring for skipping.",

  "square reports elevated prevalence of teenage pregnancy among students more than circle": "Square includes an explicit claim about pregnancy frequency: “That school has toooooooo many pregnanct girls there and that's includes freshman too!!!” Circle reviews contain no discussion of teen pregnancy or pregnancy-related prevalence.",

  "square reports concerns about early school start times more than circle": "One square reviewer complains about scheduling: “I think this school starts too early for teenagers. Most of CFISD start at the same time,” while circle includes no comments about bell times or start-of-day scheduling."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports chronic basic facilities neglect (broken toilets, no air, filthy restrooms) more than square": "Circle lists repeated, low-level facility failures and makeshift fixes: “toilets are broken, a plastic bag is placed over it,” “Water lays in the corner of Leona Middle School girls restroom,” “Rooms are not clean, dust bunnies are everywhere,” and “school is run down with no air,” whereas Square's complaints about cleanliness are framed as pests and general dirtiness rather than persistent broken fixtures and makeshift repairs.",
  "square reports pest infestations and acute health incidents (roach/rodent problems and food poisoning) more than circle": "Square explicitly states a “roach and rodent problem” and describes a daughter who “ate from the school's cafeteria and got food poisoning,” concrete acute health hazards not described in Circle.",
  "circle indicates near-absence of school-run cafeteria service and reliance on off-site paid food more than square": "Circle claims “Food has not been served at the high school for over 15 years” and that “Kids have to eat pizza everyday and have to walk to get it so be prepared to spend 25 dollars a week on lunch,” describing a de facto lack of school food service; Square, by contrast, describes a functioning cafeteria (though with some problems) — “foods in cafeteria are affordable and delicious” and only occasionally “run out of lunch to sell.”",
  "circle reports shortened instructional days and lack of instructional time causing curriculum stagnation more than square": "Circle notes “short school days only 6 hr days. Kids have to eat pizza... the teachers do not have time to teach the students properly,” and a concrete outcome: “My child is doing the same math and science I did in 7th grade... he is in 11th grade,” indicating institutional scheduling and instructional-time problems absent from Square’s descriptions of rigorous coursework.",
  "circle reports a sports-first culture that sidelines advanced academic students more than square": "Circle repeatedly says “This school is all about sports... if your child is an academic superstar there is nothing for them here” and “so much emphasis on sports that the other kids get overlooked,” framing athletics as prioritized to the detriment of advanced academics; Square praises athletics but pairs that praise with clear academic supports and clubs.",
  "square documents leadership turnover and visible administrative instability more than circle": "Square explicitly reports “three principals within three years and the current principal is on her way out,” and criticizes the principal’s communication and respect, whereas Circle complains about principal quality but gives no account of rapid leadership turnover.",
  "square documents specific staff misconduct and opaque disciplinary communication to parents more than circle": "Square names concrete incidents and secrecy: “A math teacher was recently fired for inappropriate interaction with a student yet this was never shared with the parents,” and a suspension where parents were told they “didn't need to hear what was said”; Circle criticizes policy enforcement but does not describe specific misconduct cases or intentional nondisclosure to families.",
  "square describes organized, diverse extracurricular offerings and structured academic support more than circle": "Square details “tons of different clubs, activities and sports,” a “very well rounded curriculum,” teachers with “office hours where you could do work independently with a teach[er] close by,” and explicit nurturing of students, while Circle only emphasizes athletics as the primary extracurricular and lacks descriptions of clubs or structured academic supports.",
  "square reports tuition-driven financial prioritization and parental cost concerns more than circle": "Square includes explicit financial/tuition dynamics: “Bishop Kearney only cares about money,” “parents pay full tuition,” and accuses the school of being “overpriced using the same vendors,” whereas Circle focuses on maintenance and program gaps and does not invoke tuition-driven incentives or pricing decisions.",
  "circle emphasizes teacher pedagogical incompetence and systemic academic under-preparation more than square": "Circle asserts “a handful of teachers that do not know how to teach,” that administrators’ “hands are tied,” and gives an outcome example of students being academically unprepared for college, e.g. “they will not be prepared for college… My child is doing the same math and science I did in 7th grade,” while Square primarily credits teachers with making learning easy and supporting students academically."
}"]
